provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: Comprehension: leadership
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to state the main idea in a passage about leadership.
The pupils should be able to list qualities of a good leader.
Introduction:
We have read stories about famous people in Nigeria. Today we will read about what makes a good leader.
Content:
Leadership is the ability to guide others. A good leader like our class captain must be honest and hardworking. Leaders make decisions for the group. They listen to everyone before deciding. For example, a market leader helps traders solve problems.
Class activity:
Read a passage about a school head boy. Discuss in pairs what makes him a good leader.
Evaluation questions:
What is leadership?
List two qualities of a leader.
How does a leader help a group?
Summary:
Leadership means guiding others with good qualities like honesty and hard work.

topics.title: Grammar: conjunctions
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify conjunctions in sentences.
The pupils should be able to join sentences using conjunctions.
Introduction:
We use words to connect our ideas in sentences. Today we will learn special connecting words.
Content:
Conjunctions are words that join sentences. Common ones are and, but, because, although. And adds ideas: "I like rice and I like beans." But shows contrast: "She is rich but she is not proud." Because gives reason: "He came late because traffic was bad." Although shows surprise: "Although it rained, we played football."
Class activity:
Each pupil writes two sentences and joins them with a different conjunction.
Evaluation questions:
Name three conjunctions.
Join these sentences with 'but': "He is tired. He continues working."
What does 'because' show in a sentence?
Summary:
Conjunctions are joining words that help us connect ideas smoothly in sentences.

topics.title: Grammar: direct and reported speech
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to change direct speech to reported speech.
The pupils should be able to use correct punctuation in direct speech.
Introduction:
When we tell someone what another person said, we change how we say it. Today we learn how to do this correctly.
Content:
Direct speech quotes exactly what someone says: "I am going to the market," said Mama. Reported speech tells what someone said without quotes: Mama said she was going to the market. We change pronouns and tense. We use commas and quotation marks in direct speech.
Class activity:
In pairs, change five direct speech sentences to reported speech.
Evaluation questions:
Change to reported speech: "I love Nigeria," said the teacher.
What punctuation do we use in direct speech?
How does 'I' change in reported speech?
Summary:
Reported speech tells what someone said without using their exact words and we change pronouns and tenses.

topics.title: Vocabulary: idioms
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to explain common idioms.
The pupils should be able to use idioms in sentences.
Introduction:
Sometimes we say special phrases that mean different from their words. Today we learn these interesting phrases.
Content:
Idioms are phrases with meanings different from their words. 'Break the ice' means to start a conversation. 'Piece of cake' means something is easy. 'Burning the midnight oil' means working late. For example, "The exam was a piece of cake for me" means I found it easy.
Class activity:
Each pupil chooses an idiom, explains its meaning, and uses it in a sentence about school.
Evaluation questions:
What does 'break the ice' mean?
Use 'burning the midnight oil' in a sentence.
Why do we use idioms in speech?
Summary:
Idioms are special phrases with meanings different from their individual words.

topics.title: Composition: narrative
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to plan a narrative story.
The pupils should be able to write a coherent story about their most memorable day.
Introduction:
We all have special days we remember well. Today we will learn how to write about those days.
Content:
A narrative story tells about events in order. First, think of your most memorable day. Then plan: beginning (what happened first), middle (what happened next), and end (how it finished). Use time words like first, then, next, finally. For example, "First, I woke up early. Then, I went to the beach..."
Class activity:
Plan your most memorable day using a beginning, middle and end table.
Evaluation questions:
What are the three parts of a narrative story?
Name two time words you can use in a story.
Why is planning important before writing?
Summary:
Writing a good narrative story requires planning with beginning, middle and end parts using time words.

topics.title: Letter writing: informal
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to write an informal letter to a cousin.
The pupils should be able to use correct format for informal letters.
Introduction:
We write letters to people we know well in a friendly way. Today we learn how to write to our family members.
Content:
An informal letter to a cousin has five parts: date, dear cousin, message, love, your name. We use simple language and share news. We write about our family, school, and ask about them. For example, "Dear Aisha, I hope you are well. My new puppy is very playful..."
Class activity:
Write a letter to your cousin telling them about your school's sports day.
Evaluation questions:
What is the greeting in an informal letter?
Name two things you can write about in the message part.
How do you end an informal letter to family?
Summary:
Informal letters to family members use a friendly format and simple language to share news.

topics.title: Oral English: stress and intonation
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify correct word stress in sentences.
The pupils should be able to use proper intonation in questions.
Introduction:
How we say words matters as much as the words themselves. Today we learn about stressing words and question tunes.
Content:
Word stress means saying one syllable louder in a word. For example, 'pho - to - graph' not 'PHO - to - graph'. Intonation is the rise and fall of our voice. Questions often rise at the end: "Are you coming?" Statements usually fall: "I am coming." Practice with Nigerian words like 'Ba - na - na' and 'a - MA - zing'.
Class activity:
In groups, practice saying sentences with correct stress and rising intonation for questions.
Evaluation questions:
Which syllable is stressed in 'pho - to - graph'?
How does our voice change in a question?
Why is stress important in English words?
Summary:
Correct word stress and intonation help us speak English clearly and express meaning properly.

topics.title: Literature: prose study
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to identify characters in a story.
The pupils should be able to describe the setting of a story.
Introduction:
Stories have people who act and places where things happen. Today we learn about these important story elements.
Content:
Characters are the people in a story. We identify them by their actions and words. The setting is where and when the story happens. For example, in a story about market day, characters might be traders and buyers, setting might be a busy Nigerian market at 7am.
Class activity:
Read a short story and draw the setting with characters in groups.
Evaluation questions:
What is a character in a story?
How can we identify characters?
What does setting tell us in a story?
Summary:
Characters are the people in stories and setting tells us where and when the story happens.

topics.title: Summary writing
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to pick main points from a passage.
The pupils should be able to write a one - paragraph summary.
Introduction:
Sometimes we need to tell someone the important points without saying everything. Today we learn how to do this.
Content:
A summary is a short version of a longer text. To write one: first read the passage carefully. Then identify the main ideas. Leave out small details. Finally, write the main points in one paragraph using your words. For example, a story about a boy helping his grandmother could be summarized as: "A kind boy helped his old grandmother with her farm work."
Class activity:
Read a passage about farming in Nigeria and write a four - sentence summary.
Evaluation questions:
What is a summary?
Name two steps in writing a summary.
Why should we leave out details in a summary?
Summary:
Writing a summary means picking main points from a text and writing them briefly in your own words.

topics.title: Revision and assessment
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The pupils should be able to answer questions on all topics covered this term.
The pupils should be able to demonstrate improved English skills.
Introduction:
We have learned many things in English this term. Today we will review and see how well we remember them.
Content:
Review all topics: comprehension, conjunctions, speech, idioms, narrative, letters, oral English, literature, and summaries. Practice each skill. For comprehension, identify main ideas. For grammar, join sentences correctly. For writing, plan before you write. For speaking, practice word stress. Be ready to show all you have learned.
Class activity:
Play a game where teams answer questions on different topics from the term.
Evaluation questions:
What is the difference between direct and reported speech?
Name two idioms and their meanings.
How do we plan a narrative story?
Summary:
Review helps us remember what we learned and shows us what we need to practice more.
